To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the revenue we can guarantee when the distribution is perturbed is essentially the same as when the distribution is known, and (2) the sample complexity of learning an auction is essentially the same for regular distributions and distributions with a monotone hazard rate.

(1) the optimal revenue of a mechanism is robust to adversarial perturbations in a distribution and (2) a near-optimal mechanism can be learned from samples when the distribution is only approximately known

we provide the first algorithms that can learn near-optimal auctions from samples when distributions are MHR, and that the sample complexity of such an algorithm is $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}/\epsilon^2)$, where $n$ is the number of samples and $\epsilon$ is the desired accuracy of the algorithm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following three fundamental problems: (1) what is the revenue that can be obtained with a corrupted distribution?

the following question: how much information about bidders' valuation distributions is required to learn a mechanism that is near-optimal for all distributions that are close to the original distribution.

the following question: ``How robust is learning optimal auctions?'' Our results suggest that, while learning optimal auctions is not robust to adversarial perturbations of the distribution, it can be made robust to adversarial corruptions in a population model, or to small perturbations of a distribution in a sample model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, given an approximate distribution for the bidder's valuations, we can learn an auction that achieves near optimal revenue simultaneously for all distributions that are $\alpha-$close to the approximate distribution in Kolmorgorov-Smirnof distance.

we provide a full characterization of the revenue that can be achieved with an adversarially corrupted distribution and a full characterization of how much data is required to learn near-optimal auctions for both MHR distributions and regular distributions.

we can learn a near-optimal mechanism for MHR distributions using a number of samples that is polynomial in the number of items, and that this sample complexity cannot be improved, while we can learn a revenue-maximizing mechanism for regular distributions with sample complexity that is polynomial in $n$ and $\log(1/\alpha)$, and cannot be improved by more than a factor $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)})$, where $n$ is the number of items.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

for both MHR distributions and regular distributions, our algorithms can learn a mechanism that is within $1-O(\min(\alpha, \sqrt{\alpha}))$ fraction of the optimal revenue, with sample complexity $O(\frac{1}{\alpha})$ and $O(\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}{\alpha})$ respectively, where $\alpha$ is the error parameter of the algorithm.

we provide the first robust learning results for revenue-optimal auctions, both for the population and distribution models, and we also provide the first sample complexity bounds for learning optimal auctions.

, for both regular and MHR distributions, our algorithms are robust to both distributional and adversarial perturbations, and can learn a near-optimal mechanism with sample complexity that is polynomially related to the number of bidders and the maximum number of bids per auction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can learn a revenue-optimal auction for a broad family of distributions from a small sample of the distribution, even when the distribution is adversarially pertubed or the samples are corrupted.
the robustness guarantees we obtain for the revenue of the auction are nearly optimal, and are not significantly worse than those for learning a single distribution in the same robust setting.
, in a wide variety of settings, it is possible to obtain a near-optimal revenue with a small number of samples.
